dossiers.title: Age of Wonders III
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The strategy loop combines city-building, army management and distinct hex-based tactical battles, with flanking, action points and spell interactions rewarding careful planning.
Research, hero class choices, spell unlocks and different troop types support campaign development, but veteran players criticize limited racial differentiation and opaque early information.
Tactical victories depend on unit positioning and preserving trained armies rather than just numerical strength; players value the depth and warn against careless auto-resolve.
Late campaigns can bog down under large armies, repeated sieges and many manual fights, prompting some players to rely on auto-battle despite enjoying the tactical system.
Story campaigns and city conquest create long scenarios, but timed objectives and artificial-seeming AI pressure make individual missions feel rushed or drawn out.
Some fans of earlier series entries perceive weaker faction identity and imbalanced class strengths despite the new tactical possibilities.
Players discuss competitive balance and the search for online opponents, with class asymmetry affecting their perception of fair multiplayer encounters.
Exploring ruins, clearing creature lairs and expanding cities can be absorbing, yet repeating minor battles and besieging multiple cities noticeably slows lengthy maps.
A Russian player account criticized the early localization and terminology; this reflects historical feedback, not necessarily today's localization state.

conflicts.statement: Detailed manual battles are celebrated for tactical variety but condemned by other players for slow, repetitive micromanagement over large campaigns.

dossiers.title: The Night of the Rabbit
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: A classic point-and-click structure sends players between hand-painted scenes to talk to characters, collect items and combine them to overcome environmental puzzles.
The illustrated storybook world and charming animal characters are repeatedly praised, including by players with reservations about the puzzles.
Some item combinations and later puzzles have unintuitive solutions, making experimentation or external guides feel necessary despite an appealing opening.
An initially clear fairy-tale adventure becomes more convoluted for some players during its second half, with slow movement and repeated backtracking interrupting momentum.
An atmospheric narrative about a young would-be magician in a magical animal world provides the experience's emotional hook and is cited as a reason to persist through puzzles.
A weak or vague in-game hint system can leave players without useful direction when stuck on specific inventory puzzles.
Some players find the adventure substantial and pleasant to revisit, while the slow methodical dialogue-and-item rhythm frustrates others.
Interface navigation and keyboard controls draw complaints that can aggravate an already deliberate point-and-click pace; evidence does not establish current prevalence.
Voice acting and musical atmosphere are part of the positive impression for players who enjoy a character-led story rather than an action-oriented game.

conflicts.statement: The fairy-tale story and artwork appeal even to critics, yet players disagree on whether the later plot and increasingly obtuse puzzle logic remain enjoyable.

dossiers.title: The Swapper
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Puzzles use a tool that creates up to four moving copies and lets the player swap position with them; geometry, lighting restrictions and synchronized movement drive solutions.
Later chambers can require precise sequencing and careful clone positioning; players report occasionally getting stuck for long periods before working out a solution.
The handmade clay-like visual style and isolated space-station atmosphere strongly characterize the experience and are praised even in some skeptical accounts.
An introspective science-fiction story explores identity, consciousness and the ethics of duplication, though some find its philosophical conclusions obscure or heavy-handed.
Some find fresh variations on cloning mechanics across successive rooms; others believe the central tool is exhausted before the adventure ends.
The central cloning tool does not gain extra copy slots through character upgrades; difficulty grows from more demanding room layouts and constraints.

Russian player feedback reports reliance on fan translations rather than built-in Russian text, and historical users organized a community translation; present platform availability was not independently dated.
Optional hidden achievements and story-related secrets are easy to miss without guidance, while one-save progression can complicate returning for them later.
A relatively compact single-player puzzle-platform experience alternates confined reasoning rooms with atmospheric exploration, avoiding combat-focused progression.

conflicts.statement: The cloning system is praised for ingenious late puzzle rooms but criticized by others as mechanically repetitive and insufficiently inventive.
